title: Candito Upper Lower Hypertrophy Program review
summary: NH reviews Jonnie Candito's 4-day upper/lower novice hypertrophy program. He praises Candito but criticises heavy squats and deadlifts on the same day, fixed rep ranges, too much volume for novices, optional exercises, offering front squats to beginners, and the neglect of biceps, long-head triceps, forearms, traps, rear delts and abs, calling it a hypertrophy program written by a powerlifter.

claims.claim: He respects Candito, an OG powerlifting YouTuber with a muscular physique, for documenting his back injury comeback to help others.
Novice programs must account for low work capacity and the need to learn the lifts; many share the same flaws.
About 90% of people who start training eventually quit, often discouraged by bad programs.
Naming training days (e.g. 'heavy lower') is good: decide what the day should be before designing it, not after.
Four days a week is the high end for novices; he usually has novices train 3 days a week because they aren't comfortable in the gym yet.
Fixed rep schemes are common in novice programs and he dislikes them; novices can handle some leeway.
He prefers deadlifts at 5 reps or fewer, but sets of 6 are fine for novices since they shouldn't grind to their max; 2x6 (12 reps) is good novice deadlift volume.
Heavy squats and heavy deadlifts on the same day never work: you're fried on the deadlift, form suffers and injury risk rises, especially for novices already afraid of deadlifting.
The squat is more taxing than the deadlift, with more actual loading.
If squat and deadlift share a day, make one lighter: high-bar squats with deficit or stiff-leg deadlifts, or low-bar squats with conventional deadlifts, never both at max intensity.
3 sets of 8-12 on accessories is enough for novices, who don't need massive volume.
'Squat' should mean a knee-flexion pattern; let lifters choose the variation (front, SSB, etc.) so they learn they needn't follow orthodox rules.
Novices given 3x6 on rows will butcher them; back exercises using the lower back and hamstrings need at least 6-10 reps so novices can stop when the reps get dirty.
One set of a shoulder exercise after bench makes no sense: bench doesn't fatigue the vertical-press muscles much, and overhead pressing can take lots of volume and is healthy for the shoulders.
The upper back can take a lot of volume, even for beginners.
For one set of 6 on a second back exercise, use a heavy row after pull-ups so form breakdown matters less.

Leaving novices room to choose which muscles to emphasise is good because it's their body, though misguided novices may overtrain; you learn through mistakes, and even a $1,000-a-day coach can't puppeteer you.
Two very taxing days in a row with fixed rep targets is too much for novices without work capacity: either the volume or their mental fortitude gives out.
Never give novice bodybuilders front squats unless they love them; the front rack took him ages to master painlessly and he'd reinvest those hours elsewhere.
He loves front squats because they deload the lumbar spine, emphasise the quads and help thoracic extension.
Technical hoops discourage novices; calisthenics is popular because it's accessible, and would lose many followers if beginners had to start on rings.
There's no such thing as a hypertrophy rep range; what matters is tonnage and your ability to progress.
5x8 back squats followed by 3x8 deadlifts would wreck a novice; cut squats to 3-4 sets.
Hamstring curls are good for hamstring development, but some people get knee pain from them.
He waited too long to train his calves and regrets it, but thinks novices don't need calf work; if included, superset calves with hamstring curls.
Novices offered optional exercises at the end of a session will skip them or do fluff with weights too light to matter; programs must tell them what to do.
Novices often stop sets from cardiovascular fatigue and mistake it for muscular failure.
He doesn't personally do incline or decline pressing.
Most people press too much and pull too little; the upper back has huge growth potential. After 10 years of training, adding upper-back volume made his grow like weeds.
3 sets of 10 for biceps once a week is not enough volume.

Powerlifter-written hypertrophy programs neglect the triceps long head, biceps, forearms, rear delts and traps; add at least one isolation for forearms and traps, and two for biceps and the triceps long head.
Novices can't be trusted to pick their own lift rotations; give them a choice among a few lifts or a movement pattern, then they must do it.
Supersetting chest and upper back on upper days saves time.
Linear progression (adding weight as you go) suits novices but isn't only for beginners; advanced lifters can use it too.
